reply.text:
The two commands do similar things, a single commit that contains a branch's changes, but they operate on different histories.

**`git merge --squash <branch>`** brings another branch's changes into your current branch.

- It stages all of that branch's changes as one set in your index and does **not** commit. You run `git commit` yourself to create the single commit.
- The result has no link to the source branch's commits. Git doesn't record a merge parent, so it doesn't know those commits were integrated.
- Your current branch's history is untouched; you only add one new commit on top.
- This is the usual way to fold a feature branch into `main` as one commit when you don't want a merge commit.

**Interactive rebase with squash** (`git rebase -i`) rewrites commits on your own branch.

- You mark commits as `squash` or `fixup` in the editor, and Git replaces those commits with combined ones. You can also reword, reorder, or drop commits.
- It changes the commit history of the branch you're on, so the old commit hashes disappear.
- If you've already pushed the branch, you'll need `git push --force-with-lease` afterward, and anyone else working on it has to coordinate with you.
- It's for cleaning up your work before it's shared, such as folding "fix typo" and "oops" commits into the commits they belong to.

**Practical differences**

| | `merge --squash` | `rebase -i` squash |
|---|---|---|
| Operates on | Another branch's changes, brought into yours | Commits on your current branch |
| Rewrites existing history | No | Yes |
| Creates the commit | You do, manually, after staging | Git does, during the rebase |
| Records that the branch was integrated | No | N/A |
| Typical use | Land a feature branch as one commit | Tidy your branch before review or merge |

**A gotcha with `merge --squash`:** because Git doesn't record the merge, if you later merge that same feature branch again (for example, to pick up new work on it), Git may try to re-apply commits that were already squashed in and produce conflicts or duplicate changes. Delete the feature branch after the squash, or merge only the new commits, to avoid this.
